canberra.title: The coast is calling … Crank It Up presents a free, fun festival for all
canberra.snippet: Are you ready for three massive days of vintage fashion, classic cars, live music and dance? This month marks the fifth iteration of Cran...
canberra.content:
Catch the Sydney Swing Katz dance troupe and a huge range of Aussie rock ‘n’ roll artists at this year’s Crank It Up Festival. Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

Are you ready for three massive days of vintage fashion, classic cars, live music and dance? This month marks the fifth iteration of Crank It Up Festival, a fun-filled celebration of all things rockabilly.

No less than 14 live bands will light up the Batemans Bay foreshore and local venues from 20 to 22 November. Expect a fresh take on 1950s and 60s rock ‘n’ roll from diverse, passionate musicians, including The B-Shakers, who have come all the way from Switzerland to headline their first Australia visit.

Also on the bill are the Sydney Swing Katz, Australia’s premier Charleston, swing, Lindy Hop, and rock ‘n’ roll dance troupe.

Face painting and jumping castles are on the cards for the kids, plus rock ‘n’ roll, rockabilly and swing dance classes for all experience levels. If you’re keen to laugh while you show off some leg power, join one of three Repco Garage Creeper Races on Saturday and Sunday.

Don’t miss the Late Nite DJ Party on Saturday at Oyster Cove Cocktail Bar, held right on the waterfront promenade from 11 pm until 2 am.

A great festival isn’t complete without great food. Local and interstate favourites will be in attendance, alongside a huge variety of retro market stalls selling new, handmade and pre-loved vintage fashion. Broulee Brewhouse has the 18+ crowd covered for drinks.

Classic pre-1979 cars are sure to wow the crowds as they cruise up the coastline. Friday drivers are set to travel from Corrigans to Bodalla on Friday morning, with The Poker Run from Bodalla to the Bay kicking off after lunch. Saturday afternoon brings the highly anticipated Ray White Town Cruise around the Batemans Bay CBD.

Old-school hot rods have long been a passion for Wayne Marshall. His pride and joy is a 1933 Ford coupe, rebuilt from scratch with a striking orange-and-gold facade.

“If you’re a vintage car lover living on the South Coast, this is the festival to be at,” Wayne says.

“I’m not a rock ‘n’ roller, but I keep coming back each year because the vibe is so fun. There’s a super social atmosphere that attracts all kinds of people, loads of unique cars to explore, great food, and music and dance all day.

“Crank It Up gets bigger and better every year. I can really see it turning into the South Coast equivalent of Cooly Rocks!”

Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

Photo: Wayne Marshall.

Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

Photo: Crank It Up Festival Batemans Bay.

There’s plenty to do and see on Sunday too, including a show-and-shine of more than 280 hot rods and a car cut-up by NSW Fire & Rescue.

Main stage will continue kicking off with The Rusty Mustangs and Rusty Pinto. Rusty Pinto has announced that Crank It Up will mark his final performance, so if you’ve never seen him before, this is your last chance.

Make sure to get dolled up in your most glamorous outfit – there are best-dressed awards and a beard & mo comp to get involved in. The 360-degree Crank It Up video booth will be ready to capture your style from every angle.

Ending the weekend on a high note is a free tiki-style afterparty at the Steampacket Hotel featuring Cherry Divine.

Organisers Leisa and Chris Tague launched Crank It Up in 2022 to attract people to Batemans Bay after the Black Summer bushfires. Since then, the couple’s little rock ‘n’ roll festival has grown into the biggest event of its kind for the area.

“Crank It Up is our way of giving back to our region and the community that we love,” Leisa says.

“The atmosphere is electric all weekend, and the community is very welcoming. People don’t expect such a unique blend of fashion, music, shopping, food, dance and cars.

“Crank It Up might be built around rockabilly, live music, badass cars and vintage style, but it has always been about something else too … celebrating our region and connecting great local businesses with the thousands of people who join us each year.”

Crank It Up Festival 2026 will be held on the Batemans Bay foreshore from 18 to 22 November. Entry is free! For the full program, visit Crank It Up Batemans Bay.

canberra.title: One in seven Canberra children face multiple disadvantages, ANU research finds
canberra.snippet: Canberra is one of Australia’s most prosperous cities, yet about one in seven children are growing up with multiple disadvantages a...
canberra.content:
New ANU research reveals how financial hardship, poor health and educational challenges can overlap, impacting children when they start school. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Canberra is one of Australia’s most prosperous cities, yet about one in seven children are growing up with multiple disadvantages affecting their health, education, family finances and social relationships, new research has found.

Researchers at the Australian National University (ANU) found that 14.6 per cent of ACT children born in 2006–07 were experiencing multiple disadvantages when they started school, aged five or six.

By the time they reached adolescence, at ages 14 to 15, the figure had risen slightly to 15.3 per cent.

Up to 89 per cent of children experiencing multiple disadvantage lived in low-income households, but the researchers found that financial hardship was only part of the picture.

Dr Joanne Rathbone, from ANU’s School of Medicine and Psychology, said the study looked beyond income to examine children’s health, education, access to basic necessities and opportunities to build supportive relationships.

For some children, financial hardship came alongside poor health, difficulties at school or limited opportunities to participate in activities and connect with others.

Looking at these experiences together helped researchers identify children who might have been overlooked if disadvantage was measured through household income alone.

The study also found that where children lived and their family circumstances were closely associated with disadvantage.

Children experiencing multiple disadvantage were up to three times more likely to live in the ACT’s most socio-economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods than other children.

They were also up to six times more likely to live in households receiving multiple social service benefits.

Parental education and health were significant factors, with affected children up to 2.5 times more likely to have parents with the lowest levels of completed education or experiencing poor physical or mental health.

For many, the difficulties were already evident before they had settled into school.

One in four children experiencing multiple disadvantage were developmentally vulnerable when they started school, raising questions about whether families are receiving enough support during the early years.

The research is part of a partnership between ANU and the ACT Government under the ACT Wellbeing Framework, which aims to give greater weight to community wellbeing when making policy and budget decisions.

Led by Professor Tegan Cruwys and Dr Rathbone, alongside former ANU professor Kate Reynolds, the project draws on the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ Life Course Data Initiative.

The dataset links Commonwealth and state or territory information relating to more than four million Australian children, allowing researchers to examine their circumstances at different stages of life.

Professor Cruwys said the project was the first to examine multiple forms of disadvantage across childhood and adolescence in the ACT.

“This project is the first to model the multi-dimensional nature of disadvantage in the ACT and identify potential targets for policy intervention,” she said.

While the findings show similar levels of disadvantage at school entry and during adolescence, researchers are yet to establish how many of the same children experienced hardship at both stages.

Dr Rathbone said further analysis was underway to understand why some children remained disadvantaged, others moved into or out of disadvantage and some avoided it altogether.

Those findings could help determine when support is most needed and what makes a difference to children’s circumstances.

The researchers also found that the proportion of children experiencing multiple disadvantage was slightly higher than earlier estimates, which had largely relied on economic measures.

Dr Rathbone said this showed why it was important to look at the different challenges children face, rather than assuming household income tells the whole story.

The findings could help the ACT Government assess whether existing services are reaching children dealing with several difficulties at once, including financial hardship, poor health and problems at school.

However, no specific policy changes or funding commitments have been announced as a result of the research.

Dr Rathbone said ANU was working with the government to finalise a report examining what the findings mean for policies and services.

The team also hopes the project will encourage greater use of linked government data to track how people’s circumstances change over their lives.

canberra.title: The power lunch has been reinvented, and it’s gone waterfront at Easy Oar
canberra.snippet: Do people still power lunch? You know the lunch: pencil skirts, shoulder pads, and deals done over too many drinks. Being Canberra, I bet...
canberra.content:
7 November 2026

Start the conversation

Easy Oar lives within the Red Shed on Black Mountain Peninsula. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Do people still power lunch?

You know the lunch: pencil skirts, shoulder pads, and deals done over too many drinks.

Being Canberra, I bet people still power lunch; they’ve just given up the shoulder pads.

Either way, I work from home … alone, so I don’t power lunch, but after a recent visit to Acton’s Easy Oar Cafe, I think there might be a new type of power lunch in town, and it involves counting grams of protein.

Easy Oar Cafe brings healthy dining to the waterfront in Action. Photo: Tenele Conway.

If you’ve been alive as long as me, roughly since the Jurassic era, you’ve likely counted a lot of things in your day. Grams of fat, Weight Watchers points, carbs, GI, macros, and calories … I think deep down we just like to count things.

If you gave up the fruitless act of counting years ago (fruitless – there’s another food fad … or was it only fruit?), let me catch you up: people that count now count grams of protein. Hit 100 grams a day for long enough, and you’re well on your way to annoying your friends with too much bro-talk. At 150 grams a day, you’ll ascend to a higher realm.

If ascension is your thing, Easy Oar is the fast track, with their menu outlining the grams of protein in each dish, ensuring every morsel aligns with your fitness goals.

Okay, that’s enough joking. In truth, Easy Oar manages to be health-focused while actually producing some damn good food in an enviable location.

Perched on the edge of Black Mountain Peninsula, sitting within the Red Shed, it has one of the most stunning views in Canberra, and popping in on a Saturday, I think this place might still be going under the radar.

The Vietnamese salad bowl is tasty and filling. Photo: Tenele Conway.

That’s not to say they weren’t busy; they were, but they weren’t thronging with the post-gym fitness crowd I would expect to see here during a Saturday lunch period.

As for the menu, it’s well-rounded, balancing a smattering of Canberra’s expected cafe dishes with a strong selection of fresh-focused dishes that feel perfect for the waterfront location.

The Vietnamese salad bowl is a stunner. The lemongrass-marinated chicken, which can be swapped for tofu, swims in a large bowl of vermicelli noodles, cucumber, red cabbage, cherry tomatoes, coriander, mint, pickled carrot and is topped with crunchy peanuts and crispy shallots.

Mine was unfortunately served without the Nuoc Cham sauce, but I realised too late to go and ask for it. Regardless of the omission, it was still a gorgeous meal. If you’re wondering about the protein bang for your buck, this dish sits at 39 grams of protein for a very reasonable $24.

The loaded sweet potato with spiced beef and salsa is a heartier take on healthy eating, with a nicely roasted sweet potato forming a base for a mound of spiced beef, tomato, cucumber, Greek yoghurt, feta, nigella seeds and lime, all topped with an avocado and coriander salsa. This dish will land you 36 grams of protein for $26.

The loaded sweet potato with spiced beef and salsa is a hearty take on healthy food. Photo: Tenele Conway.

If you’re thinking that grams of protein are fun but your personal jam is fibre, don’t worry, the menu also includes a breakdown of fibre, saturated fat and sodium. What you don’t get is a calorie count; maybe counting calories is too ‘deprivation lunch’, and not enough ‘power lunch’.

The wholesome fun doesn’t stop at delicious, healthy food; there’s also a wellness bar that starts with fresh-pressed juices. They’re shockingly naturally protein-free, which is made up for by the presence of the protein smoothies, and these things are the real power lunch.

Fortified with whey protein, you can pack away 52 grams of protein in a power choc smoothie for just $10. The rest of the smoothie menu suffers from fresh fruit inflation, with the tropical sunrise coming in similarly at $18 for 27 grams of protein.

If I lost you at ‘counting’, don’t worry, maths is not enforced onsite, and you can disregard all notions of numbers and smash out a bacon and egg roll, or fish and chips. That’s not to throw any shade on battered and porky friends; we all come to the table with different needs, and the call of bacon is one I rarely deny myself.

After an Easy Oar session, I think the power lunch is very much alive and well. It’s just swapped the shoulder pads and the deals for a decent hit of protein. And with the lake stretching out in front of you, there’s very little incentive to get back to the office, if you even have an office to go back to.

Easy Oar Cafe is located at 45 John Cardiff Close, Acton. They’re open 7 days a week from 7 am until 2 pm.

canberra.title: At 65, Libby is risking her savings on a dream to bring Canberra together, one stitch at a time
canberra.snippet: You don’t need to know how to knit, crochet or even buy a ball of yarn to walk into Kingston’s newest craft store. All you ne...
canberra.content:
At 65, Libby is turning her lifelong passion for craft into The Yarn Barn, a new Kingston space bringing Canberrans together through creativity, friendship and conversation. Photo: Oliver Street Photography.

You don’t need to know how to knit, crochet or even buy a ball of yarn to walk into Kingston’s newest craft store. All you need is a little time and a willingness to have a chat.

Opening on 27 November in Green Square, The Yarn Barn promises to be more than a shop. Its founder, 65-year-old Libby, wants to create a place where Canberrans of all ages can make friends, learn skills and find company.

“You won’t need to buy anything to feel welcome,” she said in a message shared by the Kingston and Barton Residents Group.

And she wants the community to help build it.

Experienced knitters and crocheters are being invited to teach classes, help beginners who get stuck on a stitch and share skills passed down through generations. Others can suggest workshops, recommend yarn brands or simply come along to learn something new.

“We are a learning community and our dream is to have all ages involved and skills passed from generation to generation,” Libby said.

She imagines a shop where a beginner can sit beside someone who has been knitting for decades, where people who work during the day can find company in the evening, and where men feel just as comfortable picking up a pair of knitting needles.

In fact, a planned Monday night session for men has already attracted considerable interest.

Thursday evenings will be set aside for Stitch and Yarn, a two-hour gathering from 6 pm where people can bring whatever they are working on, share ideas or simply enjoy a conversation over coffee. The sessions will cost $10, with discounted refreshments and products.

There will also be beginner classes, weekend workshops and opportunities to meet the people who create yarns, patterns and craft books.

But Libby hopes some of the friendships formed around those tables will lead to something beyond the shop.

Every few weeks, she wants crafters to work together on a project for people who need a helping hand. One of her first ideas is making beanies for Mother Ignacia Hospital in Soe City, West Timor, a project founded by her friends Dr David and Sue-Anne O’Rourke.

The invitation has already struck a chord. Her first social media announcement drew around 4000 views and more than 400 likes, while local crafters have offered to teach, supply products and lend a hand.

The Yarn Barn, a new Kingston space, aims to bring Canberrans together through creativity, friendship and conversation. Photo: Oliver Street Photography.

For Libby, that response has been particularly encouraging because opening The Yarn Barn is a considerable personal and financial gamble.

She has just turned 65, still works in the Australian Public Service and is recovering from double knee replacement surgery. “Like many women of my generation, I will need to work probably into my 80s,” she said.

Rather than wait for retirement, she decided to build something she could eventually transition into while continuing her regular job. The idea had been with her for years, but it was during her recovery from surgery that she finally asked herself: If not now, when?

“All I have is going into it,” she said.

Her love of crafting began at 11, when her mother, a keen knitter who also loved sewing, encouraged her to make her own clothes. Over the decades, she explored pottery, painting, patchwork and quilting before finding a particular love for crochet.

As a single mother, crafting with friends became an important source of companionship. During difficult or lonely periods, making something for others helped her find calm.

Following her knee surgery, she crocheted two baby blankets while managing the pain. “I enjoy the creative process, the way it stills your mind and there is a sense of accomplishment when you finish something,” she said.

Turning that passion into a business has brought unfamiliar challenges, from finding wholesalers to hiring staff. “I have all the ideas and NO idea !!!” she joked.

With help from business mentors, she is preparing for an opening weekend featuring country music, cookies and lucky door prizes. Her plans include craft retreats, a 24-hour charity craftathon and taking The Yarn Barn in her van to regional communities without yarn shops.

But when asked what she hopes to see in the store a year from now, Libby didn’t mention profits or sales, just “happy people”.

The Yarn Barn will open on 27 November at Green Square, Shop 30, 72 Jardine St, Kingston. Follow Yarn Barn on Facebook.

canberra.title: Upgrading existing pool facilities a higher priority for Canberrans than new builds, survey finds
canberra.snippet: New survey results show Canberrans want the ACT’s existing aquatic facilities upgraded and maintained, rather than building brand-n...
canberra.content:
7 November 2026

Start the conversation

A survey for the ACT Aquatic Strategy has found Canberra’s pools are mainly used for recreational swimming rather than specialised activities such as learning to swim or hydrotherapy. Photo: Belgravia Leisure.

New survey results show Canberrans want the ACT’s existing aquatic facilities upgraded and maintained, rather than building brand-new pools.

Consultation is open on the ACT Aquatic Strategy, designed to guide the Territory’s long-term planning and investment for the next 10 years.

It follows strong community campaigning to push the government to organise its approach to budgets for swimming facilities.

Work began in January, and community research showed 52 per cent of participants felt upgrades and maintenance were the most important areas for investment.

This was followed by warm-water pools (34 per cent), indoor leisure pools for families (32 per cent) and new aquatic facilities in growing areas (30 per cent).

It also showed Canberra’s current pools were mainly used for casual swimming and recreation (71 per cent), rather than specialised activities.

“Demand is lower for specialised activities such as learn-to-swim lessons (20 per cent), hydrotherapy and rehabilitation (15 per cent), aqua fitness classes (12 per cent), springboard or platform diving (5 per cent), squad swimming (3 per cent), and other organised aquatic sports,” the results stated.

Lap swimming for fitness and training was the second-most popular reason (45 per cent) to visit pools.

Indoor swimming locations were Canberra’s most popular pool destinations (59 per cent). About one in four respondents did not use any aquatic facility in the past 12 months.

Sports and Recreation Minister Chris Steel said the data would help guide future investment and ensure the ACT’s aquatic network serves the community for “generations to come”.

“Canberra’s aquatic facilities are some of our most valued community assets, supporting everything from family recreation and swimming lessons to rehabilitation, fitness and competitive sport,” he said.

“As our city continues to grow and change, we need a clear and sustainable plan for how our aquatic network evolves to meet future demand.”

The strategy will continue to examine options to deliver a 50-metre outdoor public pool in Woden, provide facilities for deep-water aquatic sports such as water polo and underwater rugby, assess the need for new facilities in growth areas such as West Belconnen, and conduct a condition audit of existing ACT Government aquatic facilities.

“This consultation is not about choosing one priority over another. It’s about understanding what matters most to the community and finding the right balance,” Mr Steel said.

The government is expected to engage an aquatics consultation and engagement consultant in November to lead dedicated stakeholder meetings for aquatic sports, swim schools, facility operators and community organisations.

The draft ACT Aquatic Strategy is expected to be released in March next year, and the final version in the second half of 2027.

This means the government will be unable to fulfil a committee inquiry’s recommendation to have the document ready for the 2027-28 ACT Budget.

For now, the ACT Government has called on all Canberrans to share their feedback on priorities and identify any gaps in the existing aquatic network.

Community consultation closes on 18 December.
